The retrieved set contains mutually exclusive claims: multiple sources (d1, d3, d4, d5, d6) argue that hot drinks can cool you down via increased sweating and evaporative cooling in dry heat, while others (d7, d9) advise avoiding hot drinks and present evidence that core temperature does not differ between hot and cold drinks. The conflict hinges on environmental conditions (humidity, clothing) and measurement methods.

The cited evidence yields a nuanced final answer: hot drinks can cool you down under specific, dry conditions where sweat evaporates, but they do not universally cool everyone, and some controlled studies find no core-temperature benefit.

Whether hot drinks cool you down in hot weather depends on conditions. Several studies and expert sources report that drinking a hot beverage can lower body heat storage and feel cooling when the extra sweat it triggers fully evaporates in dry heat [d1,d3,d4,d5,d6]. However, other controlled experiments found no difference in core temperature between hot and cold drinks, and public health guidance advises avoiding hot drinks during heatwaves [d7,d9]. In short, hot drinks may cool you down in hot, dry environments if sweat evaporates, but they are not guaranteed to do so and may not help in humid conditions.
